scenes.heading: Distributed Transactions: Saga & Outbox
scenes.narration: Let's tackle distributed transactions: how to keep data consistent when one business operation spans multiple services and databases.

scenes.heading: You can't hold a lock across the network
items: ACID transactions stop working across services
Two-phase commit blocks on a coordinator and doesn't scale
The answer: Saga plus Transactional Outbox, with idempotency
scenes.narration: Once a business operation spans multiple services, the classic ACID transaction stops working: you can't hold a lock across the network. Two-phase commit tries and fails to scale because participants block holding locks between prepare and commit, and a coordinator crash leaves them stuck in doubt. The practical answer is a pair of patterns, the saga and the transactional outbox, plus idempotency keys to make it all safe.

scenes.heading: How a saga runs, and unwinds
steps: Run local transactions T1, T2, up to Tn, each committing
Each step commits immediately in its own service
If step k fails, stop advancing
Run compensations Ck-1 back to C1 in reverse
Compensations semantically undo, not roll back
scenes.narration: A saga breaks the operation into a sequence of local transactions, each committing in its own service with no global lock. It advances step by step, and if a later step fails, it runs compensating transactions in reverse to semantically undo the completed work. A compensation isn't a rollback, since the original already committed and may be visible to others; it's a new forward action, like a refund offsetting a charge, and it must be idempotent because it may be retried.

scenes.heading: The Transactional Outbox
scenes.narration: The outbox solves the dual-write problem. A service that must commit to its database and publish an event risks the two diverging if one succeeds and the other fails. Here we write the business row and the event row into an outbox table inside the same transaction, so they commit together or not at all. A separate relay then reads unsent outbox rows and publishes them, marking each sent only after a confirmed publish, so a crash simply re-publishes.

scenes.text: Exactly-once delivery over a network is impossible — brokers are at-least-once, so the same event can arrive twice.
scenes.narration: Here's the reality you must design for: exactly-once delivery over a network is provably impossible. Brokers give you at-least-once delivery, so the same event can arrive twice, whether from a retried publish or a relay re-running after a crash. If your consumer just applies every event it sees, a duplicate double-applies the effect, and you double-charge a customer.

scenes.text: Idempotent consumers dedup on a key, giving effectively-once processing over an at-least-once world.
scenes.narration: The last piece is idempotency. Each consumer records an idempotency key in a dedup table, checked inside the same transaction as the effect, so a re-delivered event is detected and skipped. Saga plus outbox plus idempotency give you effectively-once processing over an at-least-once world, and eventual consistency you can actually reason about, resume, and recover, without the blocking failure modes of two-phase commit.
